title.value: Open Sesame! On the Security and Memorability of Verbal Passwords
Open Sesame! On the Security and Memorability of Verbal Passwords

abstract.value: Despite extensive research on text passwords, the security and memorability of verbal passwords-spoken rather than typed-remain underexplored. Verbal passwords hold significant potential for scenarios where keyboard input is impractical (e.g., smart speakers, wearables, vehicles) or users have motor impairments that make typing difficult. Through two large-scale user studies, we assessed the viability of verbal passwords. In our first study (N = 2,085), freely chosen verbal passwords were found to have a limited guessing space, with 39.76% cracked within 10 9 guesses. However, in our second study (n = 600), applying word count and blocklist policies for verbal password creation significantly enhanced verbal password performance, achieving better memorability and security than traditional text passwords. Specifically, 65.6% of verbal password users (under the password creation policy using minimum word counts and a blocklist) successfully recalled their passwords in long-term tests, compared to 54.11% for text passwords. Additionally, verbal passwords with enforced policies exhibited a lower crack rate (6.5%) than text passwords (10.3%). These findings highlight verbal passwords as a practical and secure alternative for contexts where text passwords are infeasible, offering strong memorability with robust resistance to guessing attacks. 720 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

Despite extensive research on text passwords, the security and memorability of verbal passwords-spoken rather than typed-remain underexplored. Verbal passwords hold significant potential for scenarios where keyboard input is impractical ( e.g., smart speakers, wearables, vehicles) or users have motor impairments that make typing difficult. Through two large-scale user studies, we assessed the viability of verbal passwords. In our first study ( N = 2,085), freely chosen verbal passwords were found to have a limited guessing space, with 39.76% cracked within 109 guesses. However, in our second study ( n = 600 ), applying word count and blocklist policies for verbal password creation significantly enhanced verbal password performance, achieving better memorability and security than traditional text passwords. Specifically, 65.6% of verbal password users (under the password creation policy using minimum word counts and a blocklist) successfully recalled their passwords in long-term tests, compared to 54.11% for text passwords. Additionally, verbal passwords with enforced policies exhibited a lower crack rate (6.5%) than text passwords (10.3%). These findings highlight verbal passwords as a practical and secure alternative for contexts where text passwords are infeasible, offering strong memorability with robust resistance to guessing attacks. 1. Introduction Passwords remain the predominant authentication method in real-world systems despite well-known security and us- ability limitations [7], [59]. User-chosen text passwords often exhibit limited entropy, making them susceptible to guessing attacks [10], [45]. Moreover, conventional text password entry requires specific input devices ( e.g., keyboards), limiting accessibility across contexts. To overcome these constraints, verbal passwords ( i.e., spoken rather than typed) are de- signed to provide an effective, hands-free alternative. This authentication approach delivers particular value in scenarios where keyboard input is unavailable or impractical: when using keyboard-less devices ( e.g., smart speakers, wearables, vehicles), when users have motor impairments that make typing difficult, or when users' hands are occupied with other tasks [30], [40], [46]. Unlike voice biometrics, which authenticates users based on vocal characteristics ( e.g., pitch, accent, cadence), verbal passwords rely on the linguistic content of a secret phrase. This approach offers several advantages: reduced input errors during activities like smartphone banking, and faster authentication compared to virtual keyboards, especially for long yet pronounceable passphrases. Verbal passwords have already gained traction in security-sensitive real-world applications, including call-based customer support systems at financial institutions, where users verify their identity by speaking predefined phrases [13], [38], [49]. They are also being integrated into emerging platforms such as virtual reality headsets [58] and smart home systems [42], [57]. Despite their potential benefits, key research questions still remain regarding the security and usability of verbal passwords; particularly how users generate secure verbal pass- words (e.g., their resistance against sophisticated guessing attacks) and how effectively users recall these passwords over time. Moreover, while previous research has demonstrated that attackers can leverage advanced language models ( e.g., Markov chains, GPT) to predict probable password struc- tures [44], [54], the effectiveness of these techniques for ver- bal passwords has not been tested empirically. Without robust guidelines (e.g., comprehensive verbal password generation policies), users may select verbal passwords with insufficient entropy, thereby replicating the fundamental vulnerabilities associated with traditional text passwords. These gaps underscore the urgent need for a compre- hensive study to assess the security and recall rates of verbal passwords in real-world scenarios. This prompts us to consider two main questions: (1) What factors do users consider when creating their verbal passwords, especially without being governed by specific password policies? and (2) How do the security and recall rates of verbal passwords compare to those of traditional text passwords? To answer these questions, we conducted two large-scale user studies involving 2,085 participants. Specifically, the first study ex- amines the security and recall rates of verbal passwords freely chosen by participants ( N = 2 ,085) without any enforced policies, providing baseline insights into their performance. The second study introduces specific password policies for both verbal and text passwords, which participants ( n = 600) must follow when creating their passwords. This allows us to compare how these policies affect security and recall rates across both password types. Moreover, we developed PassphraseGPT [17] by adapting PassGPT [54], an LLM- based password generator, to create a new model trained on 720 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00130 passphrase data. While PassGPT was originally designed to generate text-based passwords, PassphraseGPT specializes in generating and evaluating phrase-like passwords using the same architecture. Key Findings. Our research provides comprehensive insights into the security and memorability of verbal passwords, highlighting their potential as an alternative authentication method. In our first study, freely chosen verbal passwords exhibited substantial vulnerability to guessing attacks, with PassphraseGPT successfully cracking 39.76% of all pass- words within 109 guesses. Among the 907 passwords consis- tently remembered over 9 days, 40.35% remained guessable- primarily due to the prevalence of shorter passwords: 77.8% of user-chosen passwords contained three words or fewer, which significantly contributed to their susceptibility. Our second study demonstrated that password creation policies enforcing word count requirements and blocklists enhance both security and memorability for verbal passwords. Long-term memorability analysis showed that 65.45% of participants in the VP-L (Verbal Password-Length) and VP- LB (Verbal Password-Length & Blocklist) groups success- fully recalled their verbal passwords across all memory tests, compared to 54.11% in the TP-LB (Text Password- Length & Blocklist) group ( p < 0.05, Fisher's exact test with Bonferroni correction). Regarding security, verbal passwords created under the VP-LB policy had the lowest crack rate (7.5%), lower than the 10.0% for text passwords and 12.5% for verbal passwords with only a word count requirement, despite the lack of statistical significance ( p > 0.5). These findings highlight verbal passwords as a practical authentication method, particularly in scenarios where tradi- tional text passwords are impractical, such as voice-activated systems or accessibility-focused applications. Guided by appropriate policies, verbal passwords can effectively balance security and memorability, making them a viable comple- mentary solution in authentication systems. 2. Background Text-based Password. Text-based passwords have been widely used for authentication to protect online identities due to their compatibility and straightforward implementation across platforms, particularly when combined with com- plementary technologies [53], [61]. While these passwords typically combine alphanumeric characters and symbols, their security effectiveness heavily relies on length and complexity to withstand brute-force and dictionary attacks [37], [55]. However, human behavior often compromises this security: users frequently create simple, predictable passwords or reuse them across multiple accounts, creating significant vulnerabilities [4], [15]. As a result, organizations, including web service providers, have implemented password-creation policies such as length requirements, mandatory inclusion of various character types, and regular password updates [21], [23], [48]. Verbal Password. Verbal passwords are an authentication method involving users speaking a password aloud , which is then verified by matching it with a stored version. Unlike traditional text passwords entered via a keyboard, verbal passwords rely on the accuracy of spoken words for au- thentication. They consist of words or phrases that are easy to speak and remember. Verification can be handled by an automated voice recognition system ( e.g., Alexa) or by a human verifier (e.g., customer support agent) who ensures the correct words are spoken to confirm the speaker's identity. This approach is particularly useful in hands-free settings, such as with smart speakers and immersive technologies like VR/AR systems. For example, smart home security system companies such as ADT Security [2] and Norton [52] use verbal passwords to verify user's identity when interacting with monitoring centers or customer support. Additionally, financial institutions [13], [49] ask users to set up verbal passwords when opening an account. 3. Problem Statement Despite the growing interest in verbal passwords for voice-activated systems, their fundamental security properties remain little understood. While some prior research suggested that familiar words and phrases could enhance memorabil- ity [3], [39], the existing passphrase studies cannot be directly applied to verbal passwords. Unlike text-based passwords, verbal passwords must be not only memorable but also easily pronounceable and recognizable by speech recognition systems. This unique requirement likely influences how users create and choose their verbal passwords, potentially leading to a different verbal password space than traditional text passwords. However, there is insufficient empirical evidence on both user behavior in creating verbal passwords under the unique constraints and the passwords' resilience against automated cracking attempts. The absence of established policies governing verbal passwords, such as guidelines for length restrictions or blocklisting common phrases, further compounds this knowledge gap. Understanding these aspects is crucial as verbal passwords must maintain security stan- dards comparable to traditional passwords while serving as an effective authentication method. To this end, we raise the following three research questions. • RQ1: What is the guessing space of user-chosen verbal passwords, and how well do users recall them? • RQ2: How do password policies affect the guessing space and recall rates of verbal passwords? • RQ3: Can verbal passwords serve as complementary authentication solutions to traditional text passwords? To address our research questions, we conducted two large-scale user studies, outlined in Figure 1. The first study examines user behavior and password creation patterns, providing baseline insights into the security and memorability of verbal passwords. We simulated an account creation process for a mobile banking application, with participants (N = 2 , 085) creating a verbal password on their smart- phones, reflecting real-world scenarios where typing may be challenging. This study addresses RQ1 and reveals users' password creation patterns and recall, highlighting the need for effective password policies. 721
